attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his Substack post, written in his own voice.

semantics.note: 'Current AI simply isn't reliable' is an unhedged statement about the present. The drafter correctly kept it apart from the forecast clause that follows it.

contract.note: The plain reading is fair and ordinary: recurring material failures that rule out dependable use on demanding tasks without checking, not failure on every task. Choosing February 2026 as the period is the evaluator's choice, but it is reasonable for an ongoing-state claim.

evidence.note: The International AI Safety Report 2026 (3 Feb 2026) finds that current systems still fabricate information and make errors, and that failure rates cannot yet be cut to the level many high-stakes settings need. It also notes improvements, but that does not undercut the plain reading.

The HalluHard preprint (1 Feb 2026) reports about 30% hallucination for frontier models with web search. It is a deliberately hard, niche benchmark with unverified experiment dates, so it only corroborates.

reviews.rationale: An authoritative scientific assessment published in the target period says current AI's failure rates remain too high for many high-stakes uses. That meets the support condition on a fair plain reading. The reported reliability gains do not show dependable performance across demanding tasks, so the contradiction condition is not met.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his Substack post.

semantics.note: Both 'will cost lives' clauses are firm, so this is a scored forecast with no deadline. Reading it as military AI mistakes follows from the surrounding context.

contract.note: Requiring both a fatal AI error and at least one incident with clearly many deaths fits the two parts of the sentence. Requiring a causal AI error, not just AI involvement, is a fair reading of 'mistakes'.

evidence.note: A July 2026 autonomous-drone strike killed three civilians. The packet does not establish that an AI error caused it, as opposed to a flight failure, and it is not a many-lives incident.
The incident is from 2024, before the forecast, and whether AI was involved is uncertain. It cannot resolve the claim.

reviews.rationale: The forecast has no deadline, and the early-resolution rule is not met. No post-publication incident with clearly many deaths caused by a military AI error is established, and even the three-death drone case lacks a clear causal account of an AI error. Not seeing the event yet is not failure.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his Substack post.

semantics.note: 'Many people... will die, needlessly' is firm. 'Perhaps thousands' is a hedged scale and is correctly not treated as a minimum. The link to military AI comes from context, which the drafter flagged.

contract.note: Reading 'needlessly' as preventable is ordinary. Requiring a clearly numerous total, not a thousand, respects the hedge. Excluding ordinary war deaths is fair.

evidence.note: A July 2026 AI-guided drone strike killed three. The full decision chain has not been independently reconstructed, and three deaths are not 'many'.
The UN findings on Minab concern a 28 Feb 2026 strike, which is before the forecast, and they make no AI-specific causal finding.

reviews.rationale: The forecast has no deadline. The evidence shows only one post-publication incident with three deaths, and AI causation and preventability are not established for it. The early-resolution threshold of clearly numerous preventable AI-linked deaths is not met. The Minab strike predates the forecast and cannot count.
